nameStory: The Eastern Tailed-Blue gets its name from two key features: the delicate, thread-like 'tails' that extend from its hindwings like tiny streamers, and the beautiful blue coloration on the males' upper wing surfaces. While females are more brownish-gray, both sexes flash hints of that signature blue that gives all the 'blue' butterflies their collective name.
description: The Eastern Tailed-Blue is a tiny butterfly, one of our smallest in New England, with a wingspan barely larger than a quarter. Males display brilliant blue wings with dark borders, while females are more subdued in brown and gray tones. Both sexes have distinctive thin, hair-like tails projecting from their hindwings, making them look like they have delicate little streamers. The undersides of their wings are pale gray with small dark spots and often show orange eyespots near those characteristic tails.

idTips.label: Thin Wing Tails
idTips.description: Look for the thread-like extensions from the hindwings - they're thinner than pencil leads and often move in the breeze, creating the illusion of antennae at the 'wrong' end of the butterfly

idTips.label: Tiny Size
idTips.description: One of our smallest butterflies with wings that span about the width of a quarter - they flutter close to the ground with a weak, bouncy flight pattern

idTips.label: Male Blue Color
idTips.description: Males flash bright metallic blue on top when wings are open, with a silky shimmer that catches sunlight - females lack this blue and appear brownish-gray instead

idTips.label: Spotted Undersides
idTips.description: When wings are closed, both sexes show pale gray undersides decorated with small dark spots and often bright orange eyespots near the wing tails

idTips.label: Ground-Level Flight
idTips.description: They rarely fly higher than knee-level, preferring to dance among low flowers and grasses with an erratic, bouncing flight style

habitat: Eastern Tailed-Blues thrive in open, sunny areas throughout New England, especially disturbed sites like old fields, roadsides, gardens, and meadow edges. They're particularly fond of areas where legumes (plants in the pea family) grow, since their caterpillars feed on plants like clover, wild pea, and vetch. You'll often spot them in suburban areas, parks, and anywhere wildflowers bloom in full sun.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in May, with males actively patrolling low-growing flowers for mates. Look for their bouncy flight patterns among dandelions and early wildflowers.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs from June through August with multiple generations. Adults are most visible on warm, sunny days when they're actively nectaring on small flowers like clover and asters.
seasonality.fall: A final generation appears in September and early October, often smaller in number but still active on warm days. Adults die with the first hard frost.
seasonality.winter: The species overwinters as pupae (chrysalids) hidden among plant debris and leaf litter near their host plants, completely dormant until spring warmth triggers emergence.

funFact: Eastern Tailed-Blues are master mimics - those wing tails aren't just decoration, they're survival tools that create a 'false head' at the rear of the butterfly, complete with eyespots that look like eyes and tails that wiggle like antennae, confusing predators about which end to attack and giving the butterfly a split-second advantage to escape in the opposite direction!
confusionNotes: The tiny size and wing tails make this species fairly distinctive, but it can be confused with other small blue butterflies like the Spring Azure. Remember: if it has those thread-like tails, it's definitely a Tailed-Blue - other blues in our area lack these streamers entirely.
contextualKnowledge: This butterfly was formerly classified in the genus Everes, so you might see it listed as Everes comyntas in older field guides or websites. The scientific name shuffle doesn't change the butterfly, but it can confuse beginners trying to cross-reference different sources.
compareHints: The Eastern Tailed-Blue is the only member of its genus regularly found in New England - its relative the Western Tailed-Blue stays true to its name and remains in western North America. Compared to other small blues in the Gossamer-wing family, the Eastern Tailed-Blue's wing tails are the dead giveaway, as species like Spring Azures and Silvery Blues have rounded hindwings without any tail extensions.
